===== NEW MESSAGES SINCE YOUR LAST TURN =====
**Codex (Design Lead · User Advocate) — Round 1**

pulse-relay is designed as a trust-graph relay utility, not a message feed: a parent posts an urgent same-day pickup coverage request into a known pod, every action is server-confirmed, and exactly one person can hold the live claim while everyone else sees a clear “already covered” outcome.

Design language and identity:
Relay HUD is the app-level language. Beacon is the signature motion and component name, not the branding. The visual system must stay calm, legible under stress, and proof-oriented: always showing why an action is complete and exactly who did what next.

DESIGN SPEC - Type scale  
Use a single tokenized type scale in `Theme.swift`; every screen text derives from it.

- `hudTitleDisplay`: 34, heavy, mapped to `largeTitle`, lineHeight 1.05
- `hudTitlePrimary`: 30, semibold, mapped to `title`, lineHeight 1.08
- `hudTitleSecondary`: 22, semibold, mapped to `title3`, lineHeight 1.15
- `hudBodyEmphasis`: 18, semibold, mapped to `headline`, lineHeight 1.2
- `hudBody`: 17, regular, mapped to `body`, lineHeight 1.25
- `hudBodyStrong`: 16, semibold, mapped to `callout`, lineHeight 1.25
- `hudLabel`: 15, medium, mapped to `subheadline`, lineHeight 1.2
- `hudCaption`: 13, medium, mapped to `caption`, lineHeight 1.3
- `hudMicro`: 11, regular, mapped to `caption2`, lineHeight 1.3

All text labels, buttons, and timers must support Dynamic Type and use `@ScaledMetric`/`UIFontMetrics` compatible tokens where spacing is critical.

DESIGN SPEC - Spacing grid  
Base unit: 4 pt.

- `spacing.0 = 4`
- `spacing.1 = 8`
- `spacing.2 = 12`
- `spacing.3 = 16`
- `spacing.4 = 20`
- `spacing.5 = 24`
- `spacing.6 = 32`
- `spacing.7 = 40`
- `safeInsetX = 16`
- `safeInsetY = 14`
- `cardInnerV = 16`
- `cardInnerH = 16`
- `betweenComponents = 12`
- `buttonHeight = 52`
- `iconSize = 24`
- `statusDot = 10`

No fixed heights for content cards; height is adaptive to text, and no element may overlap another text block at any Dynamic Type size.

DESIGN SPEC - Semantic color palette  
All tokens in `Theme.swift`, no inline color literals outside that file.

- `surface.background`: light `#F3F7FB`, dark `#0D131B`
- `surface.card`: light `#FFFFFF`, dark `#171E29`
- `surface.strong`: light `#EAF0F7`, dark `#202A36`
- `surface.divider`: light `#D6DEE8`, dark `#2A3747`
- `text.primary`: light `#102033`, dark `#EDF4FF`
- `text.secondary`: light `#495A6C`, dark `#A3B1C0`
- `text.muted`: light `#748093`, dark `#7E8A99`
- `accent.pulse`: light `#F39D3A`, dark `#F6B45C`
- `accent.pulseDim`: light `#FFD8A6`, dark `#8A5A22`
- `state.confirmed`: light `#2BAF9E`, dark `#22B9A8`
- `state.terminalSlate`: light `#74828F`, dark `#8794A2`
- `state.terminalSurface`: light `#E9EEF5`, dark `#2A3544`
- `state.warning`: light `#DFA63A`, dark `#D79A35`
- `state.error`: light `#D84A50`, dark `#F86C71`

Constraint: true red (`state.error`) is only for network/system failures and never used for normal request outcomes such as “already covered”.

DESIGN SPEC - Corner radii  
- `radius.xs = 8`
- `radius.sm = 10`
- `radius.md = 14`
- `radius.lg = 18`
- `radius.card = 20`
- `radius.pill = 999`

DESIGN SPEC - Component inventory  
- `BeaconCard` (core): request state surfaces, pulse + latch visuals, status chip, elapsed timer; used in Relay Board and Request Detail.
- `RelayHUDHeader`: pod title, member count, settings/profile affordances.
- `PrimaryActionButton`: 52-pt CTA button with full-width variant and secondary outline variant.
- `StatusPill`: explicit textual state chip with icon + color role.
- `EmptyStatePanel`: icon + one-line explanation + single recovery action.
- `LoadingBanner`/`ErrorBanner`: compact, persistent top strip style with retry.
- `ElapsedTimerLabel`: live HH:MM:SS formatted label (“open for 02:14”).
- `RequestComposerCard`: short note field + optional urgency chip + submit.
- `DualChoiceActionPanel`: accept/release/withdraw actions with role-based visibility.
- `ConfirmSheet`: reusable confirmation modal for release/withdraw.
- `ReceiptCard`: shared internal-and-shareable projection, typography-first.
- `ShareableProjectionRow`: masked details only, no child identity, no location.
- `AuthBrandPanel`: welcome + Apple sign-in button.
- `CodeChip`: join/revoke pod invite code row with copy action.
- `SessionHintBanner`: warnings like “delivery may be delayed on this device.”

DESIGN SPEC - Navigation  
Use a single native-stack app with sheet overlays, no tabs.

- `AppGate` -> `AuthGate`  
- If signed in and podless -> `PodOnboarding`  
- Else -> `RelayBoard` as default root  
- `RelayBoard` entry points:
  - `ComposeRequest` as modal sheet
  - deep-link push into `RequestDetail` (for request id)
  - `ReceiptDetail` as modal from completed request card
- `Profile` and `PodSettings` are stack-presented secondary screens from board header, minimal and plain.

No branch-heavy feature menus. Minimal, predictable IA only.

DESIGN SPEC - Per-screen empty/loading/error states  

Auth Gate  
- Empty/signed-out: “Welcome to Relay HUD” / `person.circle` / “Continue with Apple”  
- Loading: “Checking sign-in…” with spinner and disabled actions  
- Error: “Sign-in currently unavailable.” / `wifi.exclamationmark` / “Try again”

Pod Onboarding  
- Empty/no pod:  
  - icon: `person.2.fill`  
  - copy: “You’re not in a pod yet”  
  - action: “Create pod” and “Join with invite code”  
- Create in progress: “Creating your pod…” / `shield.lefthalf.fill` / disabled actions, no fake success  
- Join in progress: “Joining pod…” / `link` / disabled actions  
- Invalid code: “That invite code is not valid.” / `exclamationmark.shield` / action: “Retry”  
- Success join/create: immediate route to `RelayBoard` with server state confirmation

Relay Board  
- Loading: shimmer cards, top CTA disabled, copy “Loading your pod state” / `hourglass` / Retry after failure
- All clear + pod-of-one empty: icon `checkmark.seal.fill`, copy “All clear,” subtitle with explicit “No other members yet” + “Share invite”
- All clear + populated pod: icon `checkmark.circle` + “No active requests” + “Post a request if you need pickup help”
- Active requests:
  - open list of `BeaconCard` items sorted by urgency then age
- Error: “Board couldn’t refresh.” / `exclamationmark.triangle` / “Retry now”

Compose Request  
- Editing/default: note field + urgency chips + “Post request”  
- Awaiting server ack: disable inputs, show “Posting request…” / subtle pulse starts only after tap  
- Success: route to board with updated card (server confirmed only)  
- Post failed: “Couldn’t post right now.” / `wifi` / “Retry”
  
Request Detail  
- Loading: skeleton card / “Loading request” / Retry
- Open + unclaimed:
  - primary action: `I can cover this pickup`
  - status in amber, timer always visible
- Awaiting acceptance/accept ack:
  - lock UI, show status “Sending confirmation…”  
- Winner confirmed:
  - teal/green latch, status text includes claimant name
- Loser already covered:
  - same latch motion and same duration, no error styling, no red, no shake  
- Reopened (after release):
  - state returns to open, pulsing only after new action ack
- Still open escalation:
  - timer badge becomes visible, action: “Re-broadcast to pod”
- Withdrawn:
  - muted slate card, no audit/receipt action
- Completed:
  - muted slate card + receipt action
- Error: “This request state could not be updated.” / `arrow.clockwise` / “Retry action”

Receipt  
- Loading: “Preparing receipt copy” / spinner  
- Loaded: internal rows + share card projection + muted placeholders for deleted members  
- Error: “Receipt not available.” / `doc.text` / “Reload receipt”

Profile  
- Empty user name state allowed; fallback initials  
- Loading profile image placeholder  
- Error only for sign-out/network: inline banner + retry

Pod Settings  
- Empty/no code scenario: “No active code” / action: “Create new code”  
- Code exists: show code chip and “Revoke and reissue”  
- Error on revoke: “The code could not be updated.” / action: “Try again”

DESIGN SPEC - Interaction states and invariant rules  
- No state is shown as “done” unless backend ack is received.
- Open/unclaimed and awaiting states are visually distinct and always show elapsed timer.
- Loser (“already covered by X”) is a successful resolution state, visually parallel to winner latch and never red/error-like.
- “Withdraw” is requester-only and unavailable after accept.
- “Release” is accepter-only and always reopens + re-notifies.
- Loading/error and empty states are designed content, never placeholders.

DESIGN SPEC - Motion & haptics  
- Open → awaiting: calm heartbeat pulse:
  - transform: scale 0.99 → 1.02 and border alpha oscillation
  - duration: 0.9s, easeInOut, repeating while awaiting
- Deterministic resolution (winner and loser) latch:
  - immediate transition into stable card state
  - duration: 0.45s
  - spring: response 0.45, damping 0.82
  - identical visual timing for winner and loser; only status copy/icon copy differs
- Arrival deep-link focus:
  - selected card highlights with 1.0 duration crossfade to destination, no large modal pop.
- Reduce Motion:
  - replace pulse and spring with 0.15s fade crossfade; keep state text/icon changes.
- Haptics:
  - `selection` on primary action tap
  - `softImpact` when server-confirmed state lands (winner/loser/release/withdraw/complete)
  - no success/error differentiation in loser vs winner haptics; avoid “failure” cues for loser.

DESIGN SPEC - Accessibility  
- VoiceOver:
  - Every icon-only control has explicit label (e.g., “Create pod”, “Add to board”, “Withdraw request”).
  - Request cards expose full status in one sentence: “Request from {member}, status, elapsed time, available action.”
- Color:
  - Never rely only on color; every state has chip text and icon label.
- Contrast:
  - all text contrast targets at or above WCAG AA equivalent for normal text against surface tokens.
- Touch target:
  - min 44×44 for all controls.
- Dynamic Type:
  - all typography scales and stack spacing uses tokenized minimum gaps (`betweenComponents` and at least `spacing.3` between text layers).
- State changes:
  - avoid destructive transitions; ensure announced transitions include status text (“Already covered by Alex”).
- Focus order:
  - status, timer, action buttons, then help text in each card.
- Safety:
  - no clipped text, no overlapping labels, all cards must adapt height at max content sizes.

Claude Design prompt / upload instruction  
No external design pass is required to execute this handoff; a builder can implement directly in SwiftUI from this spec.  
If you want a direct Claude Design run, use this upload prompt:

“Create SwiftUI wireframe and polished visual mockups for iOS app `pulse-relay` using Relay HUD language. Use tokenized `Theme.swift` with exact values provided in the spec. Build screens: Auth Gate, Pod Onboarding, Relay Board (all-clear + pod-of-one + active requests), Request Composer, Request Detail with winner/loser latch flow, Receipt, Profile, Pod Settings. Reject default List/Form/NavStack chrome. Enforce explicit loading/empty/error/success for each screen. Implement BeaconCard motion: open state heartbeat pulse, terminal winner/loser transition to a stable latch panel in 0.45s, identical motion for winner and loser (loser never styled as error). Avoid red for normal outcomes. Include high-contrast semantic colors, 2× theme variants (light/dark), 44pt hit targets, VoiceOver labels for icon-only controls, reduced-motion fallback crossfade, and no in-app chat/history feed.”

Biggest risk to preserve in the next phase: the visual truth of the “already covered by [name]” loser state. If the card reads like an error (red, shake, alert icon) even for a second, the product fails its core trust promise; this is the one screen behavior that must not drift.

**Claude (Frontend Engineer · Systems Thinker) — Round 1**

Let me put this together as a complete client-architecture-first pass at the design spec, since nobody's spoken yet this phase.

I want to start from the thing that will actually break if we get it wrong: how the client learns about state changes it didn't cause. The push notification payload must never be treated as data — Apple doesn't guarantee delivery order, a payload can arrive stale or duplicated, and treating it as truth would recreate exactly the false-confidence failure this whole app exists to eliminate. The correct pattern is: push arrival is a wake-up signal only, which triggers a targeted GET on that specific request, and the UI transitions only after that authoritative fetch resolves. That means every BeaconCard transition — whether caused by this device's own tap or a push-triggered refetch — goes through the same single reconciliation path into view state, which also means "awaiting-confirmation" (my own action, in flight) and "reconciling" (someone else's action, just learned about) can share the identical pulse visual but need to be distinct internal states, because if we collapse them a build agent will wire the reconcile path to skip the pulse and jump straight to the terminal card, which breaks the demo's whole point of watching both phones resolve in real time. I'd also add a client-side foreground refresh — on scenePhase becoming active, refetch the board — as a backstop for the honestly-documented case where APNs silently drops a push on a fresh pod's first incident; this isn't a websocket, it's a cheap correctness net, and it should not be confused with the still-open elapsed timer, which should tick locally off a stored server timestamp so we're not hammering the network just to advance a clock.

Two data-model consequences fall out of the multi-open-request decision that I don't think anyone's pinned down yet. First, ordering: if a pod can have two simultaneously open requests, the board needs a server-defined, stable sort (I'd propose oldest-created-first, since age is already the thing we're surfacing as the urgency signal) and the client must render server order verbatim rather than re-sorting locally — otherwise two devices with slightly different fetch timing show cards in different positions, which is a subtle but real ambiguity bug in an app whose entire premise is zero ambiguity. Second, offline compose: the brief already locked a "will send once connected" draft state, so the client needs a real local outbox — action IDs generated and queued the moment the user taps send/accept/release/withdraw offline, replayed in order on reconnect via NWPathMonitor, each queued action rendering a distinct "queued — sending when back online" chip that is visually and semantically different from "awaiting confirmation," because awaiting-confirmation implies an active round-trip is happening right now and queued does not. Skipping this distinction would mean either lying about network state or leaving users staring at a spinner that's actually just... waiting for wifi.

On architecture: root of the app is a state-driven switch, not a TabView — SessionGate resolves to AuthView (signed out), PodOnboardingView (signed in, no pod), or LiveBoardView (signed in, has pod) as the actual root, so there's no tab bar wasting chrome on an app with essentially one screen that matters. LiveBoardView presents the composer and request-detail as sheets; pod settings and profile are reachable via small toolbar affordances, not tabs. Deep links resolve through a single router that maps a push's request ID to "present RequestDetailSheet for X," with three sub-states of its own worth naming explicitly: the request is already synced locally (show immediately), the request isn't synced yet (show a brief loading state while fetching), and the request 404s because it was withdrawn/expired before the user opened the link (a distinct "this request is no longer open" state, not a generic error — this will happen constantly in practice since push and user attention are never perfectly synced).

For the actual system: base spacing unit 4pt, steps at 4/8/16/24/32/48 (xs/sm/md/lg/xl/xxl), card internal padding 16, inter-card gap 12, screen margin 20. Type scale, all mapped to Dynamic Type roles so they scale: Display 34/bold for the pod name on the board header, Title 28/semibold for screen titles and the receipt heading, Headline 20/semibold for card primary text (requester name, "pickup coverage needed"), Body 17/regular for notes and descriptive copy, Subhead 15/medium for status-chip labels, Caption 13/regular for member counts and timestamps, and a 15/medium monospacedDigit style specifically for the elapsed-time counter so the digits don't jitter the layout as they tick. Corner radii: 8 for chips and buttons, 16 for cards, 24 for sheet top corners. Colors, semantic roles only, light/dark: background #F5F3EF / #14171A (warm off-white rather than stark white or black — a clinical palette undercuts the "relief not alarm" emotional target from the design phase), surface #FFFFFF / #1E2226, surfaceRaised #FFFFFF-with-shadow / #262B30, textPrimary #1B1F23 / #EDEFF1, textSecondary #5B6570 / #9AA4AE, accentAmber #E8A23D / #F0AE4E (open/pulse), accentTeal #1F8A70 / #35A88A (confirmed — deliberately not a saturated stoplight green), slate #8B95A1 / #6B747E (withdrawn/complete), error #D64545 / #E8615F (system errors only, never a card outcome), hairline #E4E1DA / #2C3136.

Component inventory, named for direct SwiftUI mapping: RelayBeaconView (the card itself, owns the pulse/latch state machine — states: pulsingOpen, awaitingConfirmation, reconciling, latchedConfirmed, latchedAlreadyCovered, reopened, stillOpenAged, withdrawn, completed, queuedOffline, error), StatusChip (icon+text+color, never color-alone), ElapsedTimeLabel, PodHeaderBar, AllClearIndicator (board resting state), RelayComposerSheet, DeliveryCountLabel, ConnectionBanner (surfaces both "offline, actions queued" and "cached data may be stale" — these are different messages and shouldn't be collapsed into one generic banner), SessionGateView, PodOnboardingView, JoinCodeEntryField, InviteShareCard, RequestDetailSheet, ReceiptCardView, ProfileMinimalView, PodSettingsView.

Motion: pulse is a 1.1s ease-in-out repeating opacity/scale breathing animation; the latch is a 0.35s spring (response 0.35, damping 0.75) — fast and mechanical, not bouncy. Haptics: light impact on any tap, `.success` notification haptic on the winning latch — and I want to flag this explicitly because it's an easy copy-paste mistake — the losing "already covered" latch must fire the same calm `.success`-family haptic or none at all, never `.warning`/`.error`, since a warning buzz on your wrist while the screen shows a calm teal-styled card is a worse contradiction than a shake animation would have been.

Accessibility: every BeaconCard needs one composed VoiceOver label rather than reading child elements separately — "Pickup coverage requested by [name], status open, 4 minutes elapsed, double tap for details" — assembled server-state-first so a VoiceOver user gets the same information hierarchy a sighted user gets from color+icon+position. Minimum 44x44 hit targets throughout. The one real risk I see at the largest accessibility Dynamic Type sizes (AX3–AX5) is the card's status-chip + elapsed-timer + action-button row — at default sizes that's a horizontal row, but it will not fit at AX5, so the card needs a defined vertical-stack fallback layout, not just text truncation, and that fallback needs to actually be tested at the largest size, not assumed to "just reflow."

On the Claude Design question: I'd lean toward no external design tool for this build. The thing that actually makes or breaks this app visually — the pulse-to-latch state machine and winner/loser parity — isn't representable in a static mockup; a beautiful set of Figma frames can't prove the loser transition doesn't read as an error, only running SwiftUI code can. If the team wants a design pass anyway, I'd scope it tightly: static frames for the 9 named card states plus the two board empty states, delivered against these exact tokens, explicitly not an interactive prototype, so it can't drift into inventing a different motion language than the one already locked.

**Coordinator (Claude) — decision after round 1**

Looking at this round, both Codex and Claude showed up with strong, detailed material, but they didn't converge — they actually produced two different things that need to be reconciled next round.

**Where they agree:** the big-picture shape is identical — Relay HUD as the design language, Beacon as the pulse-to-latch motion, the same screen inventory, the same hard rule that the "already covered by [name]" loser state must share the exact same latch motion/timing as the winner with zero error styling (no red, no shake, no warning haptic), tokenized Theme.swift with light/dark hex pairs, 44×44 hit targets, VoiceOver labels assembled server-state-first, and Reduce Motion collapsing the pulse/latch to a fast crossfade. Both also agree true red is reserved strictly for system/network errors, never a normal outcome.

**Where they genuinely diverge:** Codex delivered a complete, formally-structured DESIGN SPEC hitting every required heading from the phase playbook (exact type scale, spacing grid, full color palette, radii, component inventory, navigation map, per-screen states, motion/haptics, accessibility, plus an optional Claude Design upload prompt). Claude came at it from the frontend-engineering angle and raised real gaps Codex's spec doesn't cover yet: push notifications must be treated as a wake-up signal, not data — the client should re-fetch and reconcile rather than trust the payload; there needs to be a distinct "reconciling" state (learning about someone else's action) separate from "awaiting confirmation" (my own action in flight), or a build agent will wire them together and break the two-phone demo's visual proof; multi-open-request ordering needs to be server-defined and rendered verbatim, not re-sorted client-side; the offline "will send once connected" draft state needs a real local action-ID outbox with a "queued — sending when back online" state that's visually distinct from "awaiting confirmation"; and deep-links need three named sub-states (already synced, loading, or 404'd because the request was withdrawn/expired before the link was opened). Claude also produced her own complete token set — different exact hex values, spacing steps, and type sizes than Codex's — and came down against using an external Claude Design pass at all, where Codex offered it as an optional add-on.

None of that is a fight, it's two incomplete-but-compatible passes that haven't been merged yet: one canonical numeric token set needs to be chosen (not two competing palettes), Claude's new states (reconciling, queuedOffline, deep-link-expired) need to be folded into Codex's per-screen spec, and the Claude Design question needs one answer instead of two soft positions.

CONSENSUS: NO

Next round: Codex and Claude need to pick one single set of exact token values (colors/type/spacing/radii) rather than carrying two, fold the reconciling/queued-offline/deep-link-expired states into the formal per-screen spec, and agree explicitly on whether any external Claude Design pass happens at all.

===== YOUR TURN — this is Claude talking (round 2) =====

===== YOUR HAT THIS PHASE =====
Come at this as a Frontend Engineer — your lens is client architecture, state management, navigation, offline behavior, and performance. And bring the temperament of the Systems Thinker: care about how the pieces fit, the edge cases, and the second-order consequences nobody mentioned. This is your stance for THIS phase only — lean into it and don't be a yes-man.
Continue the discussion: react to the new messages by name, defend or update your position, and push toward the best answer for this phase.
Produce a handoff a designer or builder can use directly: screen list, states, navigation, content hierarchy, visual system, components, motion notes, accessibility constraints, and a professional Claude Design prompt/upload instruction when external design is desired.

How to talk in this room:
- Write in plain, natural English, like you're in a lively group chat with two
  sharp friends. NO headings, NO numbered rubrics, NO 0-100 scores, NO
  bullet-point templates, NO sign-off line. Just talk like a person.
- Speak as exactly ONE person (yourself). Don't write the others' messages.
- Go deep and be specific. Make a real argument with concrete examples and think
  out loud. A couple of rich paragraphs, not a shallow blurb.
- React to what the others actually just said, by name (Codex / Claude /
  Gemini / any local model in the room / and the human if they chimed in).
  Quote or paraphrase their point, then build on it or push back on it.
- Genuinely try to CONVINCE the group of whatever you think is the single best
  idea right now — it does NOT have to be your own. If someone makes a better
  case, say so and change your mind out loud.
- Do NOT agree just to agree. If an idea is weak, explain why. Surface the real

response:
Codex, your spec is the more complete one and I think it should be the canonical base — the type scale, the spacing grid, the fourteen-component inventory, the navigation map, all of it is more fully worked out than what I threw down, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise just to defend my own numbers. But I want to push back hard on one specific thing in your palette before we lock it, because I don't think it's a stylistic quibble, I think it actually contradicts something the design_discussion phase already fought about and settled. Your neutrals — background `#F3F7FB`, surface.strong `#EAF0F7`, dark surface `#171E29` — all lean blue. That's exactly the "cold blue-black sci-fi/military HUD" register that got explicitly named and rejected in DEC-design_discussion-001, specifically because it makes the app read as alarming rather than calm-under-stress for a parent who's just realized they can't make pickup. Your state colors (the amber pulse, the teal confirmed) are fine and match what was locked — it's the neutral scaffolding underneath them that's quietly reintroducing the tone everyone agreed to avoid. I'd rather we warm those specific tokens — something like a warm off-white background instead of a blue-white, warm charcoal instead of blue-black for dark mode — while keeping everything else in your palette, your type scale, your spacing, and your radii exactly as you wrote them. This isn't me trying to win back my own hex values, it's flagging that we're about to ship a token file that technically satisfies "distinctive palette with light/dark hex" while quietly violating a decision that was actually argued over and locked two phases ago.

Second thing: your Relay Board active-state spec says cards are "sorted by urgency then age." I don't think we have an urgency field anywhere — go back through every decision from initial_discussion through app_features and there's no priority/severity/urgency tier on a request, just requester, note, and timestamps. If we write "urgency" into the formal spec without defining what it means or where it comes from, we're doing exactly the thing the phase rules explicitly forbid — "no adjective may stand in for a number" — and we're handing the build agent an undefined sort key it'll either invent arbitrarily or silently drop. I'd rather we just commit to what the data actually supports: sort by created-at ascending, oldest-and-therefore-most-aged request first, server-authoritative order, and the client renders it verbatim rather than re-sorting locally. That was my point from round one and I don't think anything in your spec actually disagrees with it, it just accidentally introduced a field that doesn't exist. If someone genuinely wants an urgency concept later, that's a real feature proposal for a future phase, not something to smuggle into a sort-order clause here.

Now the part I think matters most and where I want to be really explicit: your per-screen spec is thorough on states, but it's silent on how the client actually learns those states changed, and that silence is exactly where a build agent will take the shortcut that breaks the demo. Nothing in your spec says "don't trust the push payload" — and if that's not written down as an explicit rule, the fast, obvious implementation path for any competent iOS engineer is to decode the notification's userInfo dictionary and update the card directly from it, because that's less code than triggering a fetch. That's the bug I'm most worried about in this entire build, more than any color choice, because it would pass every screenshot review and even pass a casual demo, and then quietly fail the actual race-condition guarantee the whole app exists to prove, the first time APNs delivers two pushes out of order or drops one. I want this written into the spec as a hard architectural rule sitting alongside your interaction invariants: push notification arrival triggers an authoritative refetch of that specific request; the card only transitions after that fetch resolves; the payload itself is never rendered as state. And I want your Request Detail state list to explicitly carry the distinction I raised last round between "awaiting acceptance/accept ack" (this device's own action, mid-flight) and a second state for "I just learned the server already resolved this via someone else's action" — call it `reconciling` if you want a name for it — because if those two get collapsed into one internal case, the most likely implementation is that the losing device just snaps straight to "already covered" with no pulse at all, which kills the exact visual proof the two-phone demo is built around: both screens doing the same calm animation, one locking one way, one locking the other.

Same logic applies to two more states you didn't include that I don't think we can drop: `queuedOffline` for an action taken with no connection (visually and textually distinct from "awaiting confirmation" — one says "we're mid-round-trip right now," the other says "this hasn't left the device yet"), and a specific "this request is no longer open" state for a push deep-link that resolves to a request that's since been withdrawn or expired — that's going to happen constantly given how this app is actually used, someone taps a notification thirty seconds after the thing got handled, and if we don't name that state explicitly it'll get rendered as a generic error, which is scary and wrong for something that's actually a fine outcome. And since we're talking about relaunch behavior — R-018's force-quit-mid-accept test needs a home in this spec too. Cached data should render instantly on cold launch, per the local-first read rule everyone's agreed to, but it needs a subtle board-level "syncing" indicator — not per-card, a single top-level one — that persists until the first fresh fetch of that session actually lands, so a user who force-quit during a mid-flight accept doesn't see week-old cached state presented with the same confidence as fresh state.

Two small things and then I'll land on the Claude Design question. Your ElapsedTimerLabel spec says HH:MM:SS — I think that's the wrong format for what's actually a same-day, usually-sub-hour window; I'd rather it read MM:SS while under an hour and roll to "Xh Ym" past that, both because "00:14:32" is visually noisier in a small chip than it needs to be and because leading zeros on an hours field that's almost always zero is just wasted legibility. And I'd merge my ConnectionBanner idea into your SessionHintBanner rather than propose a separate component — but I want it explicit that the banner needs at least two distinct copy states under one component, "you're offline, your actions are queued" versus "connection's shaky, some pod members may not have gotten this yet," because those are different facts a user needs to act on differently and collapsing them into one vague "connection issue" string undermines the honest-delivery-count requirement we already locked as demo-critical.

On Claude Design: I said no external pass, you offered an optional prompt. I want to just close this instead of leaving two soft answers on the table — my actual reasoning is that the entire value of this design system lives in a state machine (the pulse, the latch, the parity between winner and loser), and a static mockup tool literally cannot represent that; the risk isn't "we don't have a design pass," it's "we get a gorgeous set of frames that can't prove the one thing this app is actually judged on, and someone mistakes polished statics for a validated interaction." So I'd lock it as: no external Claude Design pass for this build, we go straight from this spec into SwiftUI. I'd keep your prompt text on file as a fallback only, and only reach for it if a future iteration genuinely needs static marketing/App-Store-listing imagery, not as part of this build's design-to-code path.
